title: Apply advanced breeding practices for farm animals

lessons.title: Breeding goals and selection
lessons.html:
Start with a breeding goal

Advanced breeding means deliberately choosing which animals become parents so that each generation is better suited to the farm and the market. First decide what you want to improve: for example weaning weight and fertility in a beef herd on sourveld, milk solids in a dairy herd, fleece weight and fibre fineness in Merinos, or litter size in pigs. Too many goals at once slows progress on each.

Heritability

Some traits are passed on strongly from parents to offspring (moderately to highly heritable, such as growth rate, carcass traits and fibre diameter). Others are influenced mostly by management and environment (low heritability, such as fertility and survival). Low heritability traits improve mainly through better feeding and management, while selection still helps over time.

Tools for selection

  • Visual appraisal: functional soundness of feet, legs, mouth, udder, testes and body condition. Cull unsound animals.
  • Performance records: birth weight, weaning weight, inter-calving period, fleece weight, milk yield.
  • Breeding values (EBVs): estimates from breed society and performance-testing schemes that compare animals' genetic merit fairly across herds.
  • Fertility tests: breeding soundness evaluation of bulls and rams by a vet before the season, including scrotal circumference and semen evaluation.

Culling

Culling removes animals that do not meet the goal: open (not pregnant) females, those with poor mothering, repeated breeding problems, bad udders, broken mouths or unsound legs. Regular culling keeps herd fertility and profitability high.

lessons.title: Breeding systems and reproductive technologies
lessons.html:
Breeding systems

SystemWhat it isUse
PurebreedingMating animals of the same breedStud breeding, keeping breed type
CrossbreedingMating different breedsHybrid vigour (heterosis) for fertility, survival and growth
Line breedingMating distant relatives to concentrate a superior ancestorStuds, with care
InbreedingMating close relativesGenerally avoided; increases defects and lowers fertility

Crossbreeding is common in South African commercial beef, for example crossing an adapted indigenous or Sanga type such as Nguni or Bonsmara with a larger breed to combine hardiness with growth. Rotating bulls and keeping records of sires prevents accidental inbreeding.

Reproductive technologies

  • Artificial insemination spreads the genes of superior sires widely.
  • Oestrus synchronisation: hormonal programmes that bring a group of females into heat at a planned time, allowing fixed-time AI and a short calving season. Products and schedules must be prescribed by a vet.
  • Embryo transfer: embryos from a top female are flushed and placed into recipient females, multiplying elite females. Done by vets.
  • Sexed semen increases the proportion of heifer or bull calves.
  • Pregnancy diagnosis by rectal palpation or ultrasound, done by a vet or trained person, identifies open females early for rebreeding or culling.

These technologies only pay off with good nutrition, disease control and records. A thin cow will not respond well to synchronisation.

lessons.title: Managing the breeding season
lessons.html:
A controlled breeding season

Many extensive beef and sheep farms use a defined mating season timed so that calving or lambing occurs when veld quality is good. On summer rainfall veld this often means mating in early summer so that calves are born in spring. A short season gives even groups of young that are easier to manage, wean and market.

Before the season

  • Body condition score females and adjust feeding so they are in moderate condition. Flushing (extra feed before mating) can help ewes.
  • Breeding soundness examination of all bulls and rams by a vet.
  • Vaccinate and control parasites as per the vet's programme, well before mating.
  • Check that heifers have reached adequate size and weight before first mating.

During the season

  • Use the male to female ratio recommended for your system and the age of the males; your vet or breed society can advise.
  • Watch bulls for injury, lameness or loss of interest and replace them promptly.
  • Keep sire groups separate if you need to know parentage.

After the season

  • Remove males on the planned date.
  • Pregnancy test and decide on open females.
  • Record conception rate, calving or lambing percentage, weaning percentage and calving interval.

Safety and welfare

Breeding males are most dangerous during the season. Never work alone with bulls, boars or rams, always have an escape route, and use proper facilities. Monitor females at birth and call the vet for difficult births. Hands-on training is needed for assisting births.

Key points

  • Set a clear breeding goal and select on records, breeding values and soundness.
  • Low heritability traits such as fertility depend heavily on management.
  • Crossbreeding gives hybrid vigour; avoid close inbreeding.
  • Synchronisation, embryo transfer and sexed semen need vet input and good nutrition.
  • A short, planned breeding season with pregnancy testing improves herd fertility.
